newsitem.title: USA: Japan wants Russia kept out of G7 economic meeting.
newsitem.headline: Japan wants Russia kept out of G7 economic meeting.

text.p: Japan wants assurances from leaders of the Group of Seven leading industrial nations that Russia will continue to be kept out of their meetings on financial and economic matters, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said on Thursday.

"We are interested in seeing a consensus among G7 leaders that Russia will continue to be excluded from G7 talks on financial and macro-economic issues," he told reporters on his plane heading for Denver, where the group's annual summit starts on Friday.

Russian President Boris Yeltsin has won a seat in the three-day summit as a formal partner in talks on political and selected economic issues. But he will be excluded from a meeting on financial matters.
Russian officials have said they hope their country will get full G7 membership, making it the Group of Eight.

Hashimoto said he wanted to argue against Russia's participation in crucial economic talks in his meetings on the summit sidelines. He had meetings scheduled ahead of the summit with leaders of the United States, Britain, Germany and France, as well as Russia.

Japan's reluctance to give Russia a higher profile stems from a territorial dispute that has overshadowed ties between the two countries and blocked signing of a formal peace treaty ending Second World War hostilities.
Tokyo wants Moscow to return four remote islands in the north Pacific seized by the Red Army in 1945.

"I would like to input a piece of information in the minds of the other G7 leaders that the territorial issue is still unsolved and I will ask for their cooperation in helping Japan resolve the issue," Hashimoto said.
Japan previously opposed creation of a Group of Eight, adding Russia, but dropped its objections, fearing continued opposition might hurt its improving ties with Moscow.
Despite the territorial dispute, Russia and Japan have agreed to expand economic cooperation and step up dialogue on a range of issues.

Japanese officials said Hashimoto hoped to give Japan a higher profile at his second G7 summit by unveiling proposals on global issues including environmental preservation, combating terrorism and development aid for Africa.
"Especially, environmental issues such as global warming is very important for Japan...We are ready to play a (leading) role," he said.
Japan will host a high-profile conference on global warming in Kyoto in December, a follow-up to the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro.

The Kyoto meeting will seek agreement on legally binding cuts in greenhouse gases, but an accord appears unlikely as most countries are expected to fail to meet carbon dioxide emissions targets set at Rio.
"I would like to avoid a situation where the G8 substantially deviate from each other in their resolve to reach an agreement on the issue," Hashimoto said.
